notes:
1. Meaning of Local Government

  • Local Government refers to governance by elected institutions functioning within a limited geographical area.

These institutions deal with matters directly affecting everyday life, such as:

  • Water supply.
  • Sanitation.
  • Public health.
  • Roads.
  • Street lighting.
  • Waste management.
  • Urban planning.
  • Local markets.
  • Public amenities.
  • Local Governments constitute the third level of government below the Union and State Governments.
📌 Must-Memorise

Local Government → Third Level of Government

2. Need for Local Government

Local Government promotes:

  • Democratic decentralisation.
  • Public participation.
  • Local accountability.
  • Faster service delivery.
  • Area-specific planning.
  • Administrative efficiency.
  • Development of local political leadership.
  • Citizen participation in day-to-day governance.

3. Democratic Decentralisation

Democratic decentralisation means transfer of:

  • Functions.
  • Funds.
  • Functionaries.
  • Decision-making authority

from higher levels of government to elected local institutions.

📌 Must-Memorise

Effective Decentralisation → Functions + Funds + Functionaries

4. Importance of the Three Fs

Local bodies cannot function effectively unless they receive:

  • Functions → Clearly assigned responsibilities.
  • Funds → Adequate financial resources.
  • Functionaries → Required administrative personnel.
  • Merely creating an elected institution without these powers does not ensure meaningful self-government.

5. Local Government as a State Subject

Local Government is included in:

  • Entry 5 of the State List.
  • Seventh Schedule.
  • State Legislatures therefore possess primary legislative authority over local government institutions.
📌 Must-Memorise

State List → Entry 5 → Local Government

6. State Legislative Authority

State laws regulate institutions such as:

  • Municipal Corporations.
  • Municipal Councils.
  • Nagar Panchayats.
  • Other local authorities.
  • The Constitution now provides a minimum common framework for Urban Local Governments through Part IXA.

7. Position before Constitutional Status

Before 1992, Urban Local Bodies were governed mainly by State municipal laws.

Common weaknesses included:

  • Irregular elections.
  • Frequent supersession.
  • Weak finances.
  • Excessive State control.
  • Inadequate functional devolution.
  • Limited citizen participation.
  • Lack of constitutional protection.

8. Madras Municipal Corporation

Madras Municipal Corporation was established in:

  • 1688.
  • It is regarded in the attached notes as one of the earliest municipal corporations in India.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Madras Municipal Corporation → 1688

9. Lord Mayo's Resolution, 1870

Lord Mayo's Resolution encouraged:

  • Financial decentralisation.
  • Transfer of certain local responsibilities to local bodies.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lord Mayo → 1870 → Financial Decentralisation

10. Lord Ripon's Resolution, 1882

Lord Ripon is commonly called:

  • Father of Local Self-Government in India.

His Resolution of 1882 promoted:

  • Elected local bodies.
  • Non-official participation.
  • Local financial responsibility.
  • Decentralised administration.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lord Ripon → 1882 → Father of Local Self-Government

11. Royal Commission on Decentralisation, 1907

The Commission recommended strengthening:

  • Local institutions.
  • Municipal administration.
  • Village-level governance.

12. Government of India Act, 1919

Local Self-Government was transferred to Indian Ministers in Provinces under:

  • Dyarchy.
  • This increased Indian involvement in provincial local administration.
📌 Must-Memorise

1919 Act → Local Self-Government → Transferred Subject under Dyarchy

13. Government of India Act, 1935

  • Provincial Autonomy increased the role of Provincial Governments in local administration.
  • Local Government continued to develop primarily under provincial legislation.

14. Original Constitutional Position

  • The original Constitution did not create a detailed separate constitutional framework for Municipalities.
  • Urban Local Bodies continued under State municipal laws.
  • Unlike Panchayats under Article 40, Municipalities initially had no dedicated constitutional Part.

15. Need for Urban Constitutional Reform

Growing urbanisation increased demands relating to:

  • Housing.
  • Transport.
  • Water supply.
  • Sanitation.
  • Waste disposal.
  • Environmental protection.
  • Slum improvement.
  • Urban poverty.
  • Town planning.

16. Seventy-Fourth Constitutional Amendment

  • The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 gave constitutional status to Urban Local Governments.

It inserted:

  • Part IXA.
  • Articles 243P–243ZG.
  • Twelfth Schedule.

It came into force on:

  • 1 June 1993.
📌 Must-Memorise

74th Amendment, 1992 → Municipalities

Effective → 1 June 1993

17. Part IXA

Part IXA is titled:

  • The Municipalities.

It provides the constitutional framework for:

  • Constitution of Municipalities.
  • Composition.
  • Reservation.
  • Duration.
  • Powers.
  • Finances.
  • Elections.
  • Planning Committees.

18. Rural and Urban Constitutional Framework

Urban Local Governments:

  • Part IXA.
  • 74th Constitutional Amendment.

Rural Local Governments:

  • Part IX.
  • 73rd Constitutional Amendment.
  • Detailed Panchayati Raj coverage belongs to Chapter 16.

19. Importance of Constitutional Status

Constitutional recognition seeks to ensure:

  • Regular elections.
  • Fixed tenure.
  • Reservation.
  • Independent election supervision.
  • Financial review.
  • Institutional continuity.
  • Democratic legitimacy.

20. Institutions of Self-Government

The 74th Amendment sought to transform Municipalities into:

  • Institutions of Self-Government.

Actual functional and financial devolution nevertheless depends substantially upon:

  • State legislation.
  • State administrative action.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Constitutional Status ≠ Automatic Full Municipal Autonomy

21. Main Features of the 74th Amendment

Important provisions include:

  • Three types of Municipalities.
  • Direct election.
  • Reservation.
  • Five-year tenure.
  • Elections after dissolution.
  • State Election Commission.
  • State Finance Commission.
  • Ward Committees.
  • District Planning Committee.
  • Metropolitan Planning Committee.
  • Twelfth Schedule.

22. Article 243Q

Article 243Q provides for:

  • Nagar Panchayat.
  • Municipal Council.
  • Municipal Corporation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243Q → Three Types of Municipalities

23. Factors for Municipal Classification

The appropriate type of Municipality depends on factors such as:

  • Population.
  • Density.
  • Revenue.
  • Percentage of non-agricultural employment.
  • Economic importance.
  • Other factors specified by Governor.

24. Nagar Panchayat

Nagar Panchayat is constituted for:

  • Transitional area.

It covers an area changing from:

  • Rural character.
  • To urban character.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nagar Panchayat → Transitional Area

25. Municipal Council

Municipal Council is constituted for:

  • Smaller urban area.

It may commonly be called:

  • Municipality.
  • Municipal Council.
  • Municipal Board

depending on State law.

📌 Must-Memorise

Municipal Council → Smaller Urban Area

26. Municipal Corporation

Municipal Corporation is constituted for:

  • Larger urban area.

It generally administers:

  • Major cities.
  • Large populations.
  • Complex municipal infrastructure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Municipal Corporation → Larger Urban Area

27. Industrial Township Exception

A Municipality need not necessarily be constituted in an urban area or part of it where:

  • A major industrial establishment provides municipal services.
  • Governor declares it an Industrial Township.
  • Relevant local factors must be considered.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Article 243Q → Industrial Township Exception

28. Nagar Panchayat Functions

Typical functions include:

  • Basic roads.
  • Street lighting.
  • Sanitation.
  • Drainage.
  • Water supply.
  • Waste collection.
  • Local markets.
  • Basic town planning.
  • Exact powers depend on State law.

29. Municipal Council Structure

A Municipal Council commonly consists of:

  • Elected Councillors.
  • Chairperson or President.
  • Standing Committees.
  • Municipal Commissioner or Executive Officer.
  • Municipal staff.

30. Municipal Council Functions

Common responsibilities include:

  • Urban planning.
  • Water supply.
  • Public health.
  • Sanitation.
  • Waste management.
  • Roads.
  • Street lighting.
  • Registration of births and deaths.
  • Markets.
  • Slum improvement.
  • Local taxation.

31. Municipal Corporation Structure

A Municipal Corporation commonly includes:

  • Elected Councillors.
  • Mayor.
  • Deputy Mayor.
  • Standing Committees.
  • Municipal Commissioner.
  • Administrative departments.

32. Mayor

Mayor is generally the:

  • Political and ceremonial head of Municipal Corporation.

Method of election may be:

  • Direct.
  • Indirect.
  • Exact method depends on State law.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mayor's Election Method → Not Uniform Across India

33. Municipal Commissioner

Municipal Commissioner is generally the:

  • Administrative or Executive Head.

The Commissioner commonly supervises:

  • Administration.
  • Staff.
  • Revenue collection.
  • Implementation of resolutions.
  • Public services.
  • Development works.

34. Mayor vs Municipal Commissioner

Mayor:

  • Political head.
  • Represents elected body.
  • Presides over Corporation meetings.
  • Performs civic and ceremonial functions.

Municipal Commissioner:

  • Administrative head.
  • Implements decisions.
  • Supervises officials.
  • Manages day-to-day administration.

35. Special Purpose Urban Authorities

Urban administration may also involve:

  • Development Authorities.
  • Improvement Trusts.
  • Water Boards.
  • Housing Boards.
  • Transport Authorities.
  • Industrial Township Authorities.
  • These are not necessarily elected Municipalities.

36. Overlapping Urban Authorities

  • Multiple development and service agencies may create overlapping jurisdiction.

This can weaken:

  • Integrated planning.
  • Municipal accountability.
  • Unified urban governance.

37. Article 243R

Article 243R deals with:

  • Composition of Municipalities.

Municipal seats are generally filled by:

  • Direct election from territorial wards.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243R → Composition of Municipalities

38. Territorial Wards

Every municipal area is divided into:

  • Territorial Wards.
  • Voters elect local representatives from these wards.

Representatives may be called:

  • Councillor.
  • Corporator.
  • Ward Member.

39. Nominated Municipal Members

  • State law may provide representation for persons with special knowledge or experience in municipal administration.
  • Such nominated persons generally do not possess voting rights in municipal meetings under the constitutional framework described in the source.

40. Representation of MPs and State Legislators

State law may provide representation to:

  • Lok Sabha Members.
  • Rajya Sabha Members.
  • MLAs.
  • MLCs

whose constituencies fall wholly or partly within the municipal area.

41. Election of Municipal Chairperson

Method is determined by:

  • State Legislature through law.

Chairperson may be:

  • Directly elected by people.
  • Indirectly elected by councillors.

42. Article 243T

Article 243T deals with:

  • Reservation of seats in Municipalities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243T → Municipal Reservation

43. SC and ST Reservation

Seats are reserved for:

  • Scheduled Castes.
  • Scheduled Tribes.
  • Reservation is broadly proportional to their population in the municipal area.

44. Reservation for Women

Not less than:

  • One-third of total municipal seats

must be reserved for women.

This includes seats reserved for:

  • SC women.
  • ST women.
📌 Must-Memorise

Municipal Women Reservation → Minimum 1/3

45. Reservation of Chairperson Offices

  • Not less than one-third of offices of Municipal Chairpersons must be reserved for women in the manner prescribed by State law.
  • States may provide higher reservation.

46. Backward Class Reservation

Constitution permits State Legislatures to provide reservation for:

  • Backward Classes.

Extent and method depend on:

  • State law.
  • Constitutional requirements.
  • Judicial principles.

47. Article 243V

Article 243V deals with:

  • Disqualifications for membership.

A person who has completed:

  • 21 years

cannot be disqualified merely because he or she has not attained 25 years.

📌 Must-Memorise

Municipal Membership → General Constitutional Minimum Age → 21 Years

48. Municipal Membership Qualifications

A candidate ordinarily must:

  • Be an Indian citizen.
  • Be registered as an elector.
  • Fulfil minimum-age requirement.
  • Satisfy State-law qualifications.
  • Be free from prescribed disqualification.

49. Municipal Disqualifications

Possible grounds include:

  • Office of Profit.
  • Unsound mind declared by competent court.
  • Insolvency.
  • Loss of citizenship.
  • Corrupt electoral practices.
  • Statutory disqualifications.
  • Defection where applicable under State law.

50. Article 243U

Every Municipality ordinarily continues for:

  • Five years.

Period runs from:

  • Date appointed for its first meeting.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243U → Municipality → 5 Years

51. Election Before Expiry

Municipal election must be completed:

  • Before expiry of existing five-year term.

Purpose:

  • Ensure continuity of elected local government.

52. Election after Premature Dissolution

If Municipality is dissolved early:

  • Fresh election must ordinarily be completed within six months.
📌 Must-Memorise

Municipality Dissolved → Election within 6 Months

53. Exception to Six-Month Rule

If remaining period of dissolved Municipality is less than:

  • Six months,

fresh election need not necessarily be held solely for that short remainder.

54. Remaining Term after Fresh Election

Municipality constituted after premature dissolution ordinarily serves:

  • Remaining portion of original term.
  • It does not automatically receive a fresh five-year term.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Municipality Reconstituted after Early Dissolution → Remainder of Original Term

55. Temporary Administrator

During interval between dissolution and fresh election, State Government may appoint:

  • Administrator.
  • Special Officer.
  • Such arrangement should remain temporary.

56. Article 243W

Article 243W deals with:

  • Powers.
  • Authority.
  • Responsibilities of Municipalities.
  • State Legislature may endow Municipalities with powers necessary to function as Institutions of Self-Government.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243W → Municipal Powers and Responsibilities

57. Scope of Article 243W

Municipal responsibilities may include:

  • Economic development.
  • Social justice.
  • Urban planning.
  • Municipal services.
  • Scheme implementation.
  • Twelfth Schedule functions.

58. Twelfth Schedule

Twelfth Schedule was inserted by:

  • 74th Constitutional Amendment.

It contains:

  • 18 subjects

that may be entrusted to Municipalities.

📌 Must-Memorise

Twelfth Schedule → 18 Municipal Functions

59. Urban Planning

Twelfth Schedule includes:

  • Urban planning.
  • Town planning.
  • Regulation of urban growth.
  • Preparation of local development plans.

60. Land Use and Construction

Municipal functions may include:

  • Land-use regulation.
  • Zoning.
  • Building approvals.
  • Layout regulation.
  • Development control.
  • Building safety.

61. Economic and Social Development

Municipalities may plan for:

  • Employment.
  • Urban poverty reduction.
  • Social welfare.
  • Inclusive development.

62. Roads and Bridges

Functions may include:

  • Construction.
  • Maintenance.
  • Repair.
  • Local traffic infrastructure.

63. Water Supply

Municipal responsibilities may cover water for:

  • Domestic use.
  • Industrial use.
  • Commercial use.

64. Public Health and Waste Management

Twelfth Schedule covers:

  • Public health.
  • Sanitation.
  • Conservancy.
  • Drainage.
  • Sewage.
  • Solid waste management.
  • Disease prevention.

65. Fire Services

Municipalities may undertake:

  • Fire stations.
  • Emergency response.
  • Fire-safety regulation.

66. Urban Forestry and Environment

Municipal functions may include:

  • Urban trees.
  • Parks.
  • Green belts.
  • Environmental improvement.
  • Ecological protection.

67. Protection of Weaker Sections

Municipal welfare responsibilities may cover:

  • Persons with disabilities.
  • Economically weaker sections.
  • Other vulnerable groups.

68. Slum Improvement

Functions may include:

  • Basic services.
  • Housing improvement.
  • Sanitation.
  • Water supply.
  • Rehabilitation.

69. Urban Poverty Alleviation

Municipalities may support:

  • Livelihood schemes.
  • Skill development.
  • Shelter.
  • Social assistance.

70. Urban Amenities

Twelfth Schedule includes amenities such as:

  • Parks.
  • Gardens.
  • Playgrounds.
  • Open spaces.
  • Recreational facilities.

71. Cultural and Aesthetic Development

Municipal responsibilities may include:

  • Libraries.
  • Cultural centres.
  • Heritage conservation.
  • Community education.
  • Beautification.

72. Burial and Cremation Grounds

Municipalities may maintain:

  • Burial grounds.
  • Crematoria.
  • Electric crematoriums.

73. Animal-Related Functions

Twelfth Schedule includes:

  • Cattle pounds.
  • Prevention of cruelty to animals.
  • Stray-animal management.

74. Birth and Death Registration

Municipalities may maintain:

  • Birth records.
  • Death records.

75. Public Amenities

Functions include:

  • Street lighting.
  • Parking areas.
  • Bus stops.
  • Public conveniences.

76. Slaughterhouses and Tanneries

Municipalities may regulate:

  • Location.
  • Licensing.
  • Sanitation.
  • Public health aspects of slaughterhouses and tanneries.

77. Actual Devolution of Twelfth Schedule Functions

  • Twelfth Schedule does not automatically transfer all 18 subjects to every Municipality.

Actual devolution depends on:

  • State legislation.
  • State administrative arrangements.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Twelfth Schedule → Constitutional Functional Framework

Not Automatic Transfer of All 18 Subjects

78. Obligatory Municipal Functions

Common obligatory services include:

  • Water supply.
  • Sanitation.
  • Roads.
  • Street lighting.
  • Waste management.
  • Public health.
  • Exact classification depends on State law.

79. Discretionary Municipal Functions

Depending on resources, Municipalities may undertake:

  • Parks.
  • Libraries.
  • Cultural programmes.
  • Recreation.
  • Beautification.

80. Article 243X

Article 243X deals with:

  • Municipal taxation.
  • Duties.
  • Tolls.
  • Fees.
  • Municipal Funds.
  • State Legislature may authorise Municipalities to levy and collect specified revenues.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243X → Municipal Taxation + Municipal Funds

81. Municipal Revenue Sources

Municipal income may come from:

  • Municipal taxes.
  • User charges.
  • Licence fees.
  • Property income.
  • State grants.
  • Union and State schemes.
  • Loans.
  • Municipal bonds.

82. Municipal Taxes

Examples mentioned include:

  • Property tax.
  • Profession tax where authorised.
  • Advertisement-related levy subject to law.
  • Local levies permitted by law.
  • Service-related municipal taxes.

83. User Charges

Municipalities may charge for services such as:

  • Water.
  • Sewerage.
  • Parking.
  • Trade licences.
  • Building approval.
  • Markets.
  • Solid-waste services.

84. Grants-in-Aid

Municipalities may receive grants from:

  • State Government.
  • Union Government.
  • Finance Commission-related transfers.
  • Centrally Sponsored Schemes.
  • State development programmes.

85. Municipal Fund

State law may create:

  • Municipal Fund.
  • Municipal receipts are credited to it.

Expenditure is made according to:

  • Law.
  • Municipal Budget.
  • Applicable approval procedure.

86. Municipal Budget

Every Municipality generally prepares an annual budget containing:

  • Estimated receipts.
  • Estimated expenditure.
  • Development proposals.
  • Service-delivery priorities.

87. Municipal Borrowing

Municipalities may borrow for projects relating to:

  • Infrastructure.
  • Water supply.
  • Sewerage.
  • Roads.
  • Urban transport.
  • Capital works.
  • Borrowing is governed by State law and may require approval.

88. Municipal Bonds

  • Municipal Bonds are debt instruments used to finance urban infrastructure.

Their viability depends on:

  • Creditworthiness.
  • Financial discipline.
  • Reliable revenue.
  • Transparent accounts.

89. Common Municipal Financial Problems

Urban Local Bodies may face:

  • Weak property-tax collection.
  • Narrow revenue base.
  • Dependence on grants.
  • Poor accounting.
  • Delayed State transfers.
  • Inadequate user charges.
  • Limited borrowing capacity.

90. Article 243S — Ward Committees

Ward Committees must be constituted in every Municipality having a population of:

  • Three lakh or more.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243S → Ward Committee → Population 3 Lakh or More

91. Ward Committee Composition

A Ward Committee may cover:

  • One ward.
  • Two or more wards.

State Legislature determines:

  • Composition.
  • Territorial area.
  • Method of filling seats.
  • Other details.

92. Ward Committee Functions

Ward Committees may assist in:

  • Identifying neighbourhood needs.
  • Monitoring sanitation.
  • Reviewing water supply.
  • Reporting road damage.
  • Supervising local works.
  • Monitoring welfare schemes.
  • Encouraging citizen participation.

93. Article 243ZD — District Planning Committee

District Planning Committee is constituted at:

  • District level.

It consolidates plans prepared by:

  • Panchayats.
  • Municipalities.

It prepares:

  • Draft Development Plan for the District.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243ZD → District Planning Committee

94. DPC Composition

Not less than:

  • Four-fifths of total members

must be elected by and from among elected members of:

  • Panchayats at district level.
  • Municipalities in district.
  • Representation is broadly proportional to rural and urban population.
📌 Must-Memorise

DPC → Minimum 4/5 Elected Representation

95. DPC Functions

DPC considers:

  • Common interests of Panchayats and Municipalities.
  • Spatial planning.
  • Sharing of water and natural resources.
  • Integrated infrastructure.
  • Environmental conservation.
  • Financial resources.

96. Submission of District Plan

DPC Chairperson forwards district development plan to:

  • State Government.

97. Article 243ZE — Metropolitan Planning Committee

MPC is required for:

  • Metropolitan Area.

It prepares:

  • Draft Development Plan for Metropolitan Area.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243ZE → Metropolitan Planning Committee

98. Metropolitan Area

A Metropolitan Area generally means an area with population of:

  • Ten lakh or more

comprising:

  • One or more districts.
  • Two or more Municipalities or Panchayats.
  • Contiguous areas.

and notified by Governor.

📌 Must-Memorise

Metropolitan Area → Population 10 Lakh or More

99. MPC Composition

Not less than:

  • Two-thirds of members

must be elected by and from among:

  • Elected Municipal members.
  • Panchayat Chairpersons in metropolitan area.
  • Representation is broadly proportional to population.
📌 Must-Memorise

MPC → Minimum 2/3 Elected Representation

100. MPC Functions

MPC considers:

  • Local-body plans.
  • Common urban-rural interests.
  • Spatial planning.
  • Water and natural resources.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Environmental conservation.
  • Union and State priorities.
  • Financial resources.

101. DPC vs MPC

District Planning Committee:

  • Article 243ZD.
  • District planning.
  • Minimum 4/5 elected representation.
  • Integrates rural and urban plans.

Metropolitan Planning Committee:

  • Article 243ZE.
  • Metropolitan planning.
  • Minimum 2/3 elected representation.
  • Metropolitan population generally 10 lakh or more.

102. Article 243ZA

Municipal elections are supervised by:

  • State Election Commission.
  • Article 243ZA applies SEC framework to Municipal elections.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243ZA → Municipal Elections → State Election Commission

103. Article 243K Link

State Election Commission framework originates in:

  • Article 243K.
  • It applies to local-body elections including Municipalities through Article 243ZA.

104. State Election Commissioner

State Election Commissioner is appointed by:

  • Governor.

State Election Commission is:

  • Constitutional Authority.
  • It is not merely a State Government department.

105. SEC Functions

State Election Commission supervises:

  • Electoral rolls.
  • Election schedules.
  • Nominations.
  • Polling.
  • Counting.
  • Declaration of results.
  • By-elections.
  • Election-related directions.

106. Removal of State Election Commissioner

State Election Commissioner cannot be removed except:

  • In same manner.
  • On same grounds

as a Judge of a High Court.

📌 Must-Memorise

SEC Removal Protection → Same as High Court Judge

107. SEC Service Conditions

After appointment, SEC service conditions cannot be varied:

  • To the Commissioner's disadvantage.
  • This protects institutional independence.

108. Staff for SEC

  • Governor must make necessary staff available when requested by State Election Commission for conduct of elections.

109. Delimitation and Reservation

Ward delimitation and reservation are generally governed by:

  • State legislation.
  • State rules.
  • Authorities prescribed by law.
  • State Election Commission does not automatically control every delimitation or reservation decision.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

SEC → Conducts Elections

Do Not Assume SEC Independently Controls All Delimitation

110. SEC vs Election Commission of India

State Election Commission:

  • Local-body elections.
  • Articles 243K and 243ZA.
  • Commissioner appointed by Governor.

Election Commission of India:

  • Parliament.
  • State Legislatures.
  • President.
  • Vice-President.
  • Article 324.
📌 Must-Memorise

SEC → Panchayats + Municipalities

ECI → Parliament + State Legislature + President + Vice-President

111. Article 243Y

Article 243Y deals with:

  • Finance Commission for Municipalities.
  • It links Municipal finances with State Finance Commission established under Article 243I.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243Y → Municipal Finance Review

112. State Finance Commission

Governor constitutes State Finance Commission every:

  • Five years.

Same Commission reviews finances of:

  • Panchayats.
  • Municipalities.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Finance Commission → Governor → Every 5 Years

113. SFC Composition

  • Composition.
  • Qualifications.
  • Selection method

are determined by:

  • State Legislature through law.
  • Constitution does not prescribe identical composition for every State.

114. SFC Revenue-Sharing Role

State Finance Commission may recommend principles concerning:

  • Distribution of State taxes.
  • Duties.
  • Tolls.
  • Fees.
  • Sharing among Local Governments.

115. Assignment of Taxes

SFC may recommend revenues that may be:

  • Assigned to Municipalities.
  • Appropriated by Municipalities.
  • Shared with Municipalities.

116. Grants-in-Aid

SFC recommends principles concerning grants from:

  • Consolidated Fund of State.

Grants may support:

  • Basic services.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Equalisation.
  • Financially weaker Municipalities.
  • Performance improvement.

117. Measures to Improve Municipal Finance

SFC may recommend:

  • Property-tax reform.
  • Better revenue collection.
  • Improved user charges.
  • Accounting reforms.
  • Audit reform.
  • Reduced leakage.
  • Stronger municipal funds.
  • Predictable transfers.

118. SFC Report

State Finance Commission submits report to:

  • Governor.

Governor causes before State Legislature:

  • Recommendations.
  • Explanatory memorandum.
  • Action taken or proposed.

119. Nature of SFC Recommendations

State Finance Commission recommendations are generally:

  • Advisory.

Implementation depends upon:

  • State Government.
  • State Budget.
  • Legislation.
  • Administrative follow-up.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

State Finance Commission Recommendations → Generally Advisory

120. SFC vs Union Finance Commission

State Finance Commission:

  • Articles 243I and 243Y.
  • Constituted by Governor.
  • Reviews Panchayat and Municipal finances.
  • Recommends State-to-local transfers.

Union Finance Commission:

  • Article 280.
  • Constituted by President.
  • Reviews Union–State financial relations.
  • May recommend augmentation of State Consolidated Funds for local bodies.

121. Article 280 Link

Union Finance Commission may recommend measures to augment:

  • Consolidated Fund of a State

to supplement resources of:

  • Panchayats.
  • Municipalities.
  • Such recommendations are linked to State Finance Commission findings.

122. Article 243Z

Article 243Z provides for:

  • Audit of municipal accounts.
  • Detailed arrangements are made through State law.

123. Article 243ZB

Part IXA applies to:

  • Union Territories

subject to constitutional modifications.

124. Article 243ZC

Part IXA does not automatically apply to certain areas such as:

  • Scheduled Areas.
  • Tribal Areas.
  • Areas covered by specified special constitutional arrangements

unless Parliament provides otherwise.

125. Article 243ZF

  • Existing municipal laws continued temporarily after commencement of Part IXA.

They could continue until:

  • Amendment.
  • Repeal.
  • Modification

to bring them into conformity.

126. Article 243ZG

Article 243ZG bars ordinary court interference in:

  • Delimitation.
  • Allotment of seats.
  • Municipal electoral matters

except through:

  • Election Petition as provided by law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 243ZG → Bar to Court Interference in Municipal Elections

  • Protection of Wild Animals and Birds.

Constitutionalised:

  • Panchayati Raj Institutions.

Inserted:

  • Part IX.
  • Rural Local Government details belong to Chapter 16.

Key additions:

  • Part IXA.
  • Articles 243P–243ZG.
  • Twelfth Schedule.
  • Constitutional status to Municipalities.
  • Five-year tenure.
  • Reservation.
  • State Election Commission.
  • State Finance Commission.
  • Planning Committees.

131. Eighty-Sixth Amendment, 2002

  • Inserted Article 21A.
  • The attachment links it with local educational responsibilities where such functions are entrusted to Municipalities under State law.

132. Ninety-Seventh Amendment, 2011

  • Granted constitutional recognition to Cooperative Societies.

Municipalities may interact with urban cooperatives in:

  • Housing.
  • Credit.
  • Urban development.

133. One Hundred and First Amendment, 2016

  • Introduced GST.
  • Altered broader local fiscal environment.
  • Municipal taxation continues within State-law and constitutional framework.

134. One Hundred and Fifth Amendment, 2021

Restored State power to identify:

  • Socially and Educationally Backward Classes.

This may affect local-body reservation policy subject to:

  • Constitutional provisions.
  • Judicial requirements.

135. Kishansing Tomar v. Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad, 2006

Supreme Court held:

Municipal elections must be conducted:

  • Before expiry of five-year term.
  • Or within constitutional period after dissolution.

State Governments cannot postpone them merely for:

  • Administrative.
  • Political reasons.
  • State Election Commission must ensure timely elections.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kishansing Tomar → 2006 → Timely Municipal Elections + SEC

136. State of Uttar Pradesh v. Pradhan Sangh Kshetra Samiti, 1995

The source states:

  • Local Self-Government acquired constitutional importance after the decentralisation amendments.
  • State Legislatures must legislate within the constitutional local-government framework.

137. Union of India v. R.C. Jain, 1981

The Supreme Court explained characteristics of a Local Authority, including:

  • Separate legal existence.
  • Defined territorial jurisdiction.
  • Ability to raise local revenue.
  • Administrative autonomy.
  • Performance of public functions.
📌 Must-Memorise

R.C. Jain → 1981 → Meaning of Local Authority

138. PUCL v. Union of India, 2003

The source links the case with:

  • Voter's Right to Know.
  • Candidate disclosure.
  • Electoral transparency.
  • Its democratic principles also strengthen municipal elections.

139. K. Krishna Murthy v. Union of India, 2010

The Supreme Court held:

  • Backward Class reservation in Local Bodies is constitutionally permissible.
  • Such reservation must satisfy constitutional requirements.
  • Adequate empirical basis is important.
📌 Must-Memorise

K. Krishna Murthy → 2010 → Local-Body Reservation

140. Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority, 2010

The case concerned:

  • Urban development.
  • Land acquisition.
  • Due process.

The source highlights that urban-development authorities must:

  • Follow statutory procedure.
  • Respect property rights.
  • Act fairly and transparently.

141. Vikas Kishanrao Gawali v. State of Maharashtra, 2021

The Supreme Court required the Triple Test before OBC reservation in Local Body elections.

📌 Must-Memorise

Vikas Gawali → 2021 → OBC Reservation → Triple Test

142. Triple Test

The source identifies three requirements:

  • Constitute a dedicated Commission.
  • Collect empirical data regarding backwardness.
  • Ensure reservation remains within constitutional limits laid down by Court.

143. Suresh Mahajan v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 2022

The Supreme Court reiterated:

  • Reservation must satisfy constitutional requirements.
  • Local-body elections should not be indefinitely postponed because of reservation issues.
📌 Must-Memorise

Suresh Mahajan → 2022 → Elections Cannot Be Indefinitely Delayed

144. Common Challenges of Urban Local Bodies

Municipal institutions may face:

  • Inadequate revenue.
  • Limited taxation powers.
  • Dependence on State grants.
  • Weak functional devolution.
  • Staff shortages.
  • Overlapping development authorities.
  • Excessive State supervision.
  • Weak accounting and auditing.

145. Common Problems of State Election Commissions

Challenges may include:

  • Delayed ward delimitation.
  • Incomplete reservation exercises.
  • Shortage of staff.
  • Financial dependence.
  • State interference.
  • Delayed electoral data.
  • Litigation.

146. Common Problems of State Finance Commissions

Weaknesses may include:

  • Delayed constitution.
  • Delayed reports.
  • Poor financial data.
  • Weak implementation.
  • Irregular action-taken reports.
  • Lack of professional staff.
  • Weak coordination.
  • Limited municipal fiscal autonomy.

147. Political and Financial Decentralisation

State Election Commission supports:

  • Political decentralisation.
  • Regular elections.
  • Democratic continuity.

State Finance Commission supports:

  • Financial decentralisation.
  • Revenue sharing.
  • Fiscal strengthening.

What is Local Government? → Governance by elected institutions functioning within a limited geographical area.

Which level of government do Local Governments represent? → Third level.

What are the three essential elements of effective decentralisation? → Functions, Funds and Functionaries.

Which Entry contains Local Government? → Entry 5 of State List.

Which Schedule contains State List? → Seventh Schedule.

Which Municipal Corporation is highlighted in the source as an early municipal institution? → Madras Municipal Corporation.

When was Madras Municipal Corporation established? → 1688.

Which Governor-General's Resolution of 1870 promoted financial decentralisation? → Lord Mayo.

Who is called Father of Local Self-Government in India? → Lord Ripon.

Which year is associated with Lord Ripon's Resolution? → 1882.

Which Commission of 1907 dealt with decentralisation? → Royal Commission on Decentralisation.

Under which Act did Local Self-Government become a transferred subject under Dyarchy? → Government of India Act, 1919.

Which Amendment constitutionalised Urban Local Governments? → 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.

When did it come into force? → 1 June 1993.

Which Part was inserted? → Part IXA.

What is Part IXA titled? → The Municipalities.

What is its Article range? → Articles 243P–243ZG.

Which Schedule was inserted? → Twelfth Schedule.

How many municipal functions are in Twelfth Schedule? → 18.

Which Article provides three types of Municipalities? → Article 243Q.

What are they? → Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council and Municipal Corporation.

What is a Nagar Panchayat? → Municipality for a transitional rural-to-urban area.

What is a Municipal Council? → Municipality for a smaller urban area.

What is a Municipal Corporation? → Municipality for a larger urban area.

What special exception exists under Article 243Q framework? → Industrial Township.

Who may declare an Industrial Township? → Governor.

Which Article deals with composition of Municipalities? → Article 243R.

How are municipal ward representatives generally elected? → Directly by people.

Who determines method of election of Municipal Chairperson? → State Legislature through law.

Is Mayor election method uniform throughout India? → No.

Who is generally political head of a Municipal Corporation? → Mayor.

Who is generally administrative head? → Municipal Commissioner.

Which Article deals with reservation? → Article 243T.

For which groups is constitutional reservation provided? → SCs, STs and women.

What minimum share of seats must be reserved for women? → Not less than one-third.

Does this include SC/ST women? → Yes.

Can States provide reservation for Backward Classes? → Yes.

Which Article deals with duration of Municipality? → Article 243U.

What is municipal tenure? → Five years.

When should election normally be held before natural expiry? → Before expiry of five-year term.

If Municipality is dissolved early, within how long should election ordinarily be held? → Six months.

What is the exception? → If remaining term is less than six months.

Does newly constituted Municipality after premature dissolution receive a fresh five years? → No, ordinarily only remainder of original term.

Which Article deals with disqualification? → Article 243V.

What age protection is provided under Article 243V according to the source? → A person who has completed 21 years cannot be disqualified merely for not attaining 25 years.

Which Article deals with municipal powers and responsibilities? → Article 243W.

Does Twelfth Schedule automatically transfer all 18 functions? → No.

Who actually devolves powers? → State Legislature through law.

Which Article deals with municipal taxation? → Article 243X.

Name important municipal revenue sources. → Taxes, user charges, licence fees, property income, grants, loans and municipal bonds.

What is a Municipal Bond? → Debt instrument used by Urban Local Bodies to finance infrastructure.

Which Article provides Ward Committees? → Article 243S.

In which Municipalities are Ward Committees constitutionally required? → Those having population of three lakh or more.

Which Article provides District Planning Committee? → Article 243ZD.

What does DPC integrate? → Panchayat and Municipal plans.

What proportion of DPC members must be elected as stated in the source? → Not less than four-fifths.

To whom is District Development Plan forwarded? → State Government.

Which Article provides Metropolitan Planning Committee? → Article 243ZE.

What is the population threshold stated for Metropolitan Area? → Ten lakh or more.

What proportion of MPC members must be elected? → Not less than two-thirds.

What does MPC prepare? → Draft Development Plan for Metropolitan Area.

Which Article deals with municipal elections? → Article 243ZA.

Which body conducts municipal elections? → State Election Commission.

Which Article provides the general SEC framework? → Article 243K.

Who appoints State Election Commissioner? → Governor.

How can State Election Commissioner be removed? → In same manner and on same grounds as a High Court Judge.

Can SEC service conditions be varied to disadvantage after appointment? → No.

Does SEC necessarily control all ward delimitation and reservation decisions? → No; this depends on State law.

Which Article establishes Election Commission of India? → Article 324.

Which elections does ECI conduct? → Parliament, State Legislature, President and Vice-President.

Which elections does SEC conduct? → Panchayats and Municipalities.

Which Article deals with State Finance Commission for Municipalities? → Article 243Y.

Which Article establishes State Finance Commission framework? → Article 243I.

Who constitutes State Finance Commission? → Governor.

How often? → Every five years.

Which institutions' finances are reviewed by SFC? → Panchayats and Municipalities.

What does SFC recommend? → Revenue sharing, assignment of taxes, grants and measures to improve local finances.

Are SFC recommendations automatically binding? → No; generally advisory.

To whom does SFC submit report? → Governor.

Before which institution are SFC recommendations and explanatory memorandum laid? → State Legislature.

Which Article establishes Union Finance Commission? → Article 280.

Can Union Finance Commission recommend augmentation of State Consolidated Funds for local bodies? → Yes.

Which Article deals with audit of Municipal accounts? → Article 243Z.

Which Article applies Part IXA to Union Territories? → Article 243ZB.

Which Article excludes certain Scheduled and Tribal Areas? → Article 243ZC.

Which Article preserves existing municipal laws temporarily? → Article 243ZF.

Which Article bars ordinary judicial interference in municipal electoral matters? → Article 243ZG.

Through what mechanism can municipal election disputes ordinarily be challenged? → Election Petition as provided by law.

Which case is most important for timely municipal elections? → Kishansing Tomar v. Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad, 2006.

What did Kishansing Tomar establish? → Municipal elections must be held within constitutional time limits and cannot be postponed merely for administrative or political reasons.

Which case explains characteristics of Local Authority? → Union of India v. R.C. Jain, 1981.

Which case dealt with Backward Class reservation in Local Bodies? → K. Krishna Murthy v. Union of India, 2010.

Which case established the Triple Test for OBC local-body reservation? → Vikas Kishanrao Gawali v. State of Maharashtra, 2021.

What are the three parts of the Triple Test stated in the attachment? → Dedicated Commission, empirical data, and compliance with constitutional reservation limits.

Which case stated elections cannot be indefinitely postponed because of reservation issues? → Suresh Mahajan v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 2022.

Which case dealt with urban planning and land acquisition? → Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority, 2010.

What is the most important constitutional amendment for Urban Local Government? → 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
